title: Electric Charge and Electric Field
summary: ## Electric charge
Charge is a scalar quantity measured in coulombs. It is quantized, q = ne with e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, so −1 C contains 1/e = 6.25 × 10¹⁸ electrons. Charge is conserved and additive.
Bodies are charged by friction, by conduction (contact) and by induction. A neutral pith ball touched to a negatively charged rod becomes negatively charged.
## Coulomb's law
F = (1/4πε₀) q₁q₂/r², where 1/4πε₀ = 9 × 10⁹ N m²/C² and ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C²/N m².

In a medium of dielectric constant K the force becomes F/K, so F_air : F_medium = K : 1. If both charges and their separation are halved, the force is unchanged. Two identical spheres with +2Q and −Q touched together share +Q/2 each; when replaced at the same distance they repel with F/8.
The laws of electrostatics are Coulomb's law, Gauss's law and conservation of charge. Ampère's law belongs to magnetism.
## Electric field

The electric field E = F/q₀ is the force per unit positive test charge. It is a vector with unit N/C or V/m and dimensions MLT⁻³A⁻¹. The test charge is taken as q₀ → 0 so that it does not disturb the charges producing the field.

The field of a point charge is E = q/4πε₀r². The superposition principle gives the net field as the vector sum. For a square with alternating charges (−Q, Q / Q, −Q), opposite corners carry equal charges, so the field at the centre is zero.
An oil drop of charge ne and mass m is held still when neE = mg, so E = mg/ne.
## Electric field lines

Field lines start on positive charges and end on negative ones. They never cross. Their tangent gives the direction of E, they are crowded where E is strong, and they meet a conductor at right angles.
## Electric dipole
A dipole is two equal and opposite charges a small distance 2a apart. Its dipole moment p = q × 2a, in C m, points from −q to +q.
Field on the axis: 2p/4πε₀r³. Field on the equatorial line (perpendicular bisector): p/4πε₀r³. Both fall off as 1/r³.
In a uniform field a dipole feels torque τ = p × E (magnitude pE sin θ) but no net force. Stable equilibrium is when p is parallel to E. In a non-uniform field it feels both a torque and a net force.
## Gauss's theorem

Electric flux φ = E · A has unit N m²/C = V m. Gauss's theorem: the total flux through a closed surface = q_enclosed/ε₀. It does not depend on the size of the surface, so concentric spheres round q have equal flux. Zero flux means zero net enclosed charge, but E need not be zero everywhere on the surface.

Applications: an infinite plane sheet has E = σ/2ε₀ on each side. A uniformly charged spherical shell has E = q/4πε₀r² outside and zero inside; the potential inside is constant. The field at the centre of a uniformly charged ring is zero.

objective: (a) Name the physical quantity whose SI unit is V m. (b) A neutral pith ball is connected by a copper wire to a negatively charged rod. What charge does it acquire?
Fill in the blanks: (a) Electric potential is a ______ quantity. (b) A ring of radius R carries charge q; the field at its centre is ______.
Fill in the blanks: (a) The total flux through a closed surface is ______ times the charge enclosed. (b) Electric field lines never ______ each other.
State True or False: (a) A dipole in a uniform field experiences no net force. (b) Charge is quantized.

(a) True — only a torque.
(b) True — q = ne.
Spheres A (+2Q) and B (−Q) attract with force F. They are touched and replaced. (a) Charge on each = ______. (b) New force = ______.

(a) (2Q − Q)/2 = +Q/2 each.
(b) k(Q/2)²/r² = kQ²/4r² = F/8, now repulsive (F = 2kQ²/r²).
Give one word: (a) The unit of electric dipole moment. (b) The field of a dipole on its axis varies as 1/r to the power ______.
vsa: Define electric dipole moment. Give its SI unit.
The product of either charge and the distance between them, p = q × 2a, directed from −q to +q. SI unit: coulomb metre (C m).
How does an electric dipole behave in a non-uniform electric field?
The forces on its two charges are unequal, so it feels a net force (it moves towards the stronger field when aligned) as well as a torque that tends to align it with the field.
The electric flux through a Gaussian surface is zero. Does it mean that (a) the charge enclosed is zero and (b) the field is zero everywhere on the surface?

(a) Yes — by Gauss's theorem φ = q/ε₀, so the net charge enclosed is zero.
(b) Not necessarily — field lines may enter and leave, giving zero net flux even where E ≠ 0 (e.g. a surface near an outside charge).
Draw graphs showing how E and V vary with distance r from the centre of a uniformly charged spherical shell of radius R.

E: zero for r < R, maximum at r = R, then falling as 1/r² outside.
V: constant (= q/4πε₀R) inside and on the shell, then falling as 1/r outside.
Why is the test charge taken very small (q₀ → 0) when defining the electric field?
A large test charge would exert forces on the source charges and disturb their positions, changing the very field being measured. Taking q₀ → 0 ensures the field measured is that of the source alone.
sa: Two large plane sheets with charge densities σ and −2σ are parallel and a distance d apart. Find the field (a) to the left of the first sheet, (b) to the right of the second and (c) between them.

Each sheet gives E = |σ|/2ε₀, away from a positive sheet and towards a negative one. Take +x to the right.
(a) Left: σ sheet gives σ/2ε₀ to the left; −2σ sheet gives σ/ε₀ to the right. Net σ/2ε₀ to the right.
(b) Right: σ/2ε₀ to the right and σ/ε₀ to the left. Net σ/2ε₀ to the left.
(c) Between: σ/2ε₀ + σ/ε₀ = 3σ/2ε₀, towards the −2σ sheet.

or: Show that a dipole p at angle θ to a uniform field E experiences a torque τ = p × E.

Forces +qE and −qE are equal and opposite, so the net force is zero, but they form a couple.
Torque = force × perpendicular distance = qE × 2a sin θ = pE sin θ.
In vector form τ = p × E; it tends to align p with E.

sa: What are electric field lines? State three properties. Draw them for a single positive charge and for a dipole.

Field lines are imaginary curves whose tangent at any point gives the direction of the field there.
Properties: (1) they start on positive and end on negative charges; (2) two lines never cross; (3) they are dense where the field is strong; (4) they meet a conductor's surface at right angles.
Positive charge: straight lines pointing radially outward. Dipole: lines curve from +q round to −q.
Show that the electric field of a short dipole at a point on its perpendicular bisector varies inversely as the cube of the distance.

At distance r on the bisector, each charge is √(r² + a²) away, with field kq/(r² + a²).
The components along the bisector cancel; the components parallel to the axis add: E = 2kq a/(r² + a²)^(3/2) = kp/(r² + a²)^(3/2).
For a short dipole (a ≪ r): E = p/4πε₀r³, so E ∝ 1/r³ (directed opposite to p).
la: State Gauss's theorem. Use it to find the field due to (a) an infinite plane sheet of charge and (b) a uniformly charged spherical shell at points outside and inside.

Gauss's theorem: the total electric flux through any closed surface = q_enclosed/ε₀.
(a) Plane sheet (σ): take a cylinder through the sheet. Flux passes only through the two end faces: 2EA = σA/ε₀ ⇒ E = σ/2ε₀, uniform and independent of distance.
(b) Shell (charge q, radius R):
Outside (r > R): a sphere of radius r gives E × 4πr² = q/ε₀ ⇒ E = q/4πε₀r², as if all the charge were at the centre.
Inside (r < R): no charge is enclosed ⇒ E = 0.
Define electric field at a point. Explain field lines and derive the field due to a dipole on its axial line.

Electric field E = F/q₀ (q₀ → 0), the force per unit positive test charge; unit N/C or V/m.
Field lines show the direction of E, start on + and end on − charges, and never cross.
Axial field at distance r from the centre of a dipole (±q, 2a apart): E = kq/(r − a)² − kq/(r + a)² = kq × 4ar/(r² − a²)².
For a short dipole (a ≪ r): E = 2p/4πε₀r³ along p.
